frontier.hypothesis: There exists a pure-C construct that gives the 640-valued pseudo TWO surviving sets (so birthing_insn_p returns 0 and sched1 leaves its definition at the block head) while keeping that pseudo DISTINCT from the 240 and 128 pseudos and costing ZERO extra instructions. This is now the entire remaining search: the s3 diagnostic pin already proved that once 640 holds $v1 with target's statement order, every store lands in target's slot.
frontier.mechanism: birthing_insn_p (tools/gcc-2.7.2/sched.c:2516) gates the LAUNCH_PRIORITY sink on reg_n_sets[REGNO] == 1, where reg_n_sets is computed by flow.c's life analysis (which runs BEFORE combine and sched1 in this build - dump order rtl/jump/cse/loop/flow/combine/sched). Two sets therefore have to survive cse, loop and cse2 to be counted. s6 measured that a redundant duplicate assignment does not survive cse2, and that reusing one variable for two different constants survives but collapses the two constants onto one hard register. The untried middle ground is a pseudo whose two sets carry the SAME value 640 but arise from expressions cse cannot prove equal at the second set - e.g. a value round-tripped through something opaque - or a second set that combine folds INTO an existing insn (so it is counted by flow but emits no instruction of its own, since flow runs before combine).
frontier.next_probe: Work directly against the gate rather than against the emitted asm. (i) Instrument cheaply: for each candidate form, dump with s6/rtlc.sh and read (a) how many (set (reg:HI N) (const_int 640)) insns survive into base.i.flow, (b) the ';; insn[N]: priority' line for the 640 set in base.i.sched, and (c) the greg disposition of that pseudo. A form is on the right track the moment the 640 set's priority stays 1 and greg reports it in reg 3. (ii) Enumerate second-set spellings that survive cse2: assignment of 640 through a second variable that is then copied (copy propagation may or may not merge the pseudos - check reg_n_sets, not the asm); an assignment sequenced so that the OT load sits between the two sets (cse's value table is invalidated across a may-alias memory read, which is exactly what the D_800A374C load is for these stores - this is the most promising and is genuinely untried); and 640 written as two different but equal expressions. (iii) If flow really does count a set that combine later folds away, a second set placed where combine can absorb it would be zero-cost - test by counting sets in base.i.flow versus base.i.combine for a deliberately foldable spelling. Score any survivor with s5/scoreforms.py first, then confirm with sandbox --disable all.

frontier.hypothesis: The 640 allocno can be pushed off $v0 from the ALLOCATION side instead of the scheduling side: force some OTHER pseudo that local-alloc places before it to occupy $v0 across the post-load group, with target's statement order and no extra instructions.
frontier.mechanism: local-alloc allocates allocnos in density order (short, heavily-referenced ranges first) and gives each the first non-conflicting hard register, which on this target is $v0. s6 measured that the OT-base pseudo does NOT take $v0 - greg reports it 'in 4' in every form, i.e. it is steered to $a0 by the argument it feeds - and that with target's statement order nothing else is live across the post-load group in $v0. But the OT pseudo's steering to $a0 is a preference, not a constraint, and target's own code loads the OT base straight into $a0, so the lever is not that pseudo. What has NOT been examined is whether the ot_Link ARGUMENT pseudos (the q copy, which greg reports 'in 5' = $a1) or the p pointer can be arranged so that one intermediate genuinely occupies $v0 across the post-load group at zero instruction cost.
frontier.next_probe: Read base.i.lreg/base.i.greg for the incumbent and target-order forms side by side and list, for every pseudo, its live range in sched-output insn numbers and its allocated hard reg (a ~15-line table). Then ask which pseudo could be made to span the post-load group without adding an insn. If the table shows that NO pseudo can (the likely answer, since target's post-load group is six stores plus a move and every register in it is already accounted for), record that as a closed second axis and let the reg_n_sets axis carry the function - that negative is itself worth banking, because it proves the allocation side is not reachable and the scheduling gate is the only door.

frontier.hypothesis: initPolyG4's real prototype returns the primitive pointer (inherited s5 frontier item, still unexecuted and now cheap to settle).
frontier.mechanism: A call return value is defined by the call insn itself and lives in $v0 by ABI, which would change the post-call block's live-in set. Note that s6's measurements make this LESS likely to help than s5 assumed: any pointer live across the ot_Link call must be callee-saved ($s0), so the returned value cannot stay in $v0 across the post-load group, and target's $v0 is demonstrably free there. It should therefore be settled cheaply and then dropped rather than grinded.
frontier.next_probe: Grep every caller of initPolyG4 in src/ and read the target asm of two or three of them in asm/funcs/ to see whether any consumes $v0 after the jal. If none does, the hypothesis dies immediately and cheaply and should be recorded KILLED so no later session re-opens it; if some caller does consume $v0, declare 'extern u8 *initPolyG4(u8 *p);' and measure both 'p = initPolyG4((u8 *)D_800A38B4);' and the argument-copy variant with s5/scoreforms.py, watching the 640 pseudo's greg disposition rather than just difflines - and sandbox the other callers before proposing a tree-wide signature change.
